verdict.rationale: Corporate vocal song by the gathered people is commanded across both testaments with grammar that closes the door on solo or platform-only readings. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16 the participles (the 'ing' verbs like 'speaking', 'teaching') are plural and the addressee is the reciprocal pronoun 'to one another' (heautois, heautous, G1438), so the singing is mutual address within the gathered body using 'psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais). In Hebrews 13:15 'let us offer up' (anapheromen, G0399) is a first person plural cohortative (a 'let us' verb form summoning the group to act together), offering 'a sacrifice of praise' (thysian aineseos) as a body. The verb 'to sing hymns' (hymneo, G5214) marks the Last Supper hymn at Matthew 26:30 and Mark 14:26, the prison singing at Acts 16:25, and Christ singing in the midst of the assembly at Hebrews 2:12 (quoting Psalm 22:22). In Psalm 95:1 to 2 the cohortatives 'let us sing for joy', 'let us shout', 'let us come before' (neranenah, nariah, neqademah, H7321, H6923) and the related noun 'songs' (zemirot, H2158) summon the assembly to sing together; 'to sing' (shir, H7891) and 'to make music' (zamar, H2167) carry the same plural praise-summons across the Psalms. The word 'primary' in the proposition is a comparative ranking the lexicon does not itself adjudicate, isolated in stem_audit, so the verdict affirms the strong pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) corporate-singing pattern the texts carry.

scripture.reasoning: 'Speaking to one another' (lalountes heautois) pairs the plural present participle 'speaking' (laleo, G2980, an ongoing 'ing' verb form for the whole group) with the reciprocal pronoun 'to one another' (heautois, G1438), so the song is mutual address within the gathered body, not solo or platform performance. The triad 'psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais, G5568, G5215, G5603) names three sung forms, and the closing participles 'singing and making melody with your heart to the Lord' (adontes kai psallontes te kardia hymon to kyrio, G0103, G5567) direct the singing to the Lord from the heart of the assembly addressed in the plural 'your' (hymon).

'Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly' (ho logos tou Christou enoikeito en hymin plousios, with 'let it dwell' (enoikeito, G1774) a third person imperative, a command meaning 'let it happen') governs 'teaching and admonishing one another' (didaskontes kai nouthetountes heautous, G1321, G3560, G1438), two plural participles ('ing' verbs covering the whole group) of teaching and admonishing one another, with the same triad 'psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs' (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais) and the closing 'singing with grace in your hearts to God' (adontes en chariti en tais kardiais hymon to theo). The grammar makes the song corporate, instructive, and reciprocal within the body.

'Let us offer up' (anapheromen, G0399) is a first person plural present subjunctive (a 'let us' form summoning the whole group to act together as an ongoing practice), taking 'a sacrifice of praise' (thysian aineseos, G2378, G0133), glossed as 'the fruit of lips that confess his name' (karpon cheileon homologounton to onomati autou). The 'let us' verb frames vocal praise as a continual corporate offering. 'Praise' (ainesis) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire New Testament), but its sense is fixed here by the surrounding phrase that explains it as vocal confession.

Hebrews quotes Psalm 22:22 in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, LXX) with 'I will sing your praise' (hymneso se, G5214, a future active indicative meaning 'I will sing hymns to you' as a simple statement of future fact) 'in the midst of the assembly' (en meso ekklesias). The lexical force places Christ himself singing among the gathered congregation, anchoring sung praise inside the corporate gathering as the messianic pattern.

'And having sung a hymn they went out' (kai hymnesantes exelthon, G5214, with 'having sung' an aorist active participle plural, a completed past action done together by the whole group). The participle is plural, so Jesus and the disciples sing together at the close of the Last Supper. Mark 14:26 carries the identical wording, a double witness to communal singing as the gathered response to the meal.

'I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also' (psalo to pneumati, psalo de kai to noi, G5567, future active indicative, a simple statement of intention). Paul makes singing a deliberate corporate act done with both spirit and mind in the assembly. The first person verb sits inside the gathered-church discourse of 1 Corinthians 14, where every act is for 'building up' (oikodome, the edification of the body).

'When you come together, each one has a psalm' (hotan synerchesthe, hekastos psalmon echei, G5568). The setting is explicitly 'coming together' (synerchomai), the gathered assembly, and 'a psalm' (psalmos) is one of the contributions named as belonging to each member. The grammar of the distributive 'each one' (hekastos) plus the gathered-assembly context makes congregational singing a participatory act of the body.

'Is anyone among you suffering, let him pray. Is anyone cheerful, let him sing praise' (kakopathei tis en hymin, proseuchestho. euthymei tis, psalleto, G5567, with 'let him sing praise' (psalleto) a third person imperative, a command 'let him do it'). Singing is paired with prayer as a normal mode of believer response, addressed to anyone within the plural 'among you' (en hymin) community.

'Let us go' (leku), 'let us sing for joy' (neranenah), and 'let us shout' (nariah, H7321) are first person plural cohortatives ('let us' verb forms summoning the whole group to act together). The ETCBC-BHSA (a Hebrew Bible syntax database) clause function marks these as predicate verbs (the main action verbs of the sentence) in a hortatory summons (a call to action), calling the assembly as a body to sing aloud to the LORD, the rock of our salvation.

'Let us come before' (neqademah, H6923) his presence and the parallel 'let us shout' (nariah, H7321) continue the first person plural cohortatives ('let us' verb forms summoning the group), with 'with thanksgiving' (betodah, H8426) and 'with songs' (bizmirot, H2158) naming the sung means. The corporate first person plural plus the song nouns confirm communal vocal praise as the mode of approach.

'Sing to the LORD a new song, sing to the LORD all the earth' (shiru laYHWH shir hadash, shiru laYHWH kol haarets, H7891, with 'sing' (shiru) a plural masculine imperative, a command directed at a whole group). The verb is plural imperative and the addressee is the entire earth, the broadest possible corporate body, with the same pattern repeated at Psalm 98:1 and Psalm 149:1. This anchors corporate sung praise pan-canonically (spread across the whole Bible) across the Psalms.

complicating_texts.resolution: This text counts trained temple musicians skilled in song with instruments, showing specialist instrumental and choral music inside Old Testament worship. It could be read against the proposition word 'primary', since it shows a parallel non-congregational musical mode. It is resolved by noting that the New Testament anchor texts (Ephesians 5:19, Colossians 3:16, 1 Corinthians 14:26) shift the locus of song to the whole gathered body using reciprocal pronouns ('to one another') and plural participles ('ing' verbs covering the whole group), and the lexicon does not itself rank instrumental versus vocal as primary, so this text broadens the worship-music picture without overturning the corporate-singing pattern that the 'let us' verbs and reciprocal participles command.

The 'thank offering' (todah, H8426) here is tied to sacrificial ritual rather than song, so it could narrow 'todah' to ritual sacrifice alone. It is resolved by observing that Psalm 95:2 and Hebrews 13:15 carry 'thanksgiving' (todah) and 'praise' (ainesis) into the realm of vocal praise ('the fruit of lips', karpon cheileon), confirming that the praise-offering vocabulary extends to sung confession of the gathered people.

'Take away from me the noise of your songs' (haser meali hamon shireka, using H7892, a noun for 'song', a derivative related to H7891 'to sing') is a prophetic rejection of song. It could be read as a lexical counter to corporate singing. It is resolved by noting that the rebuke targets song offered without justice (compare Amos 5:24), not the act of singing itself, and the wider canon continues to command sung praise after this oracle, so the term is contextual, not categorical.

variants.note: The New Testament anchor texts (Ephesians 5:19, Colossians 3:16, Hebrews 13:15, Hebrews 2:12, Matthew 26:30) carry editorial markers in the bundle morphology (for example the 'singing' (ado) and 'making melody' (psallo) word order and the 'to one another' (heautois) reading in Ephesians 5:19, and the article 'the' placement in Colossians 3:16), but none of these readings touches the corporate, vocal, mutual-address force of the passages. No variant units were supplied for examination, and the Psalms anchors are outside ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) scope.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that limits public worship to elements Scripture explicitly commands still affirms corporate singing, since the 'let us' verb forms ('let us sing for joy', 'let us shout', 'let us come before' (neranenah, nariah, neqademah)) and plural participles ('ing' verbs covering the whole group) with reciprocal pronouns ('speaking to one another', 'teaching one another' (lalountes heautois, didaskontes heautous)) make sung congregational praise an expressly commanded act.

A reading that permits whatever Scripture does not forbid likewise affirms corporate singing as a clearly attested mode, though it would not derive the comparative word 'primary' from the lexicon either, since the texts command congregational song without ranking it against instrumental or specialist forms.

A reading that restricts sung content to canonical psalms still affirms corporate singing, since the same anchor texts that name 'psalms' (psalmoi) name the activity as congregational. The lexical question of whether 'hymns and spiritual songs' (hymnois and odais pneumatikais, G5215, G5603) are non-psalm compositions or sub-categories of the Psalms is a separate scope question the words alone do not settle.

hermeneutics.notes: Both testaments use first person plural ('we', 'let us') and reciprocal ('one another') grammar to make song a corporate act, so the analogy of Scripture (reading the Bible by the Bible) and progressive revelation (the unfolding of teaching from earlier to later books) move in the same direction from the Psalm 95 'let us' verbs (cohortatives) and Psalm 96:1 plural commands (imperatives) to the New Testament body-building participles ('ing' verbs covering the whole group) and the Last Supper 'having sung a hymn' (hymnesantes).

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Corporate vocal singing by the gathered people is a commanded mode of Christian worship.
stem_audit.notes: The proposition word 'primary' asserts a comparative ranking of congregational singing above other musical modes (instrumental, choral, solo). The lexical data establishes that corporate vocal song is a commanded and pervasive mode of worship across the canon, but it does not itself rank that mode as first relative to others; 1 Chronicles 25:7 and the Levitical instrumental worship show specialist instrumental music coexisting in Old Testament worship, and the New Testament corpus does not contain a comparative ranking verb. The verdict is derived on the original proposition and affirms the strong pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) corporate-singing pattern, while this audit isolates 'primary' as the comparative loading the lexicon does not adjudicate.

lay_summary: Five passages set the pattern for how the gathered people of God make music. In Ephesians 5:19 Paul writes 'speaking to one another' (lalountes heautois), joining the plural participle ('ing' verb covering the whole group) to the reciprocal pronoun 'to one another' (heautois), then names 'psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs', and closes with the whole assembly singing and making melody in the heart to the Lord. Colossians 3:16 repeats the pattern: 'teaching and admonishing one another' (didaskontes kai nouthetountes heautous) through psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs as the word of Christ dwells richly among them. The grammar in both places makes song a mutual, corporate act of the body, not solo or platform performance. Hebrews 13:15 uses the first person plural 'let us offer up' (anapheromen) 'a sacrifice of praise' (thysian aineseos), called 'the fruit of lips', presenting vocal praise as a continual communal offering. The Last Supper closes with 'having sung a hymn' (hymnesantes), a plural participle covering Jesus and the disciples together (Matthew 26:30, Mark 14:26), and Hebrews 2:12 has the risen Christ himself saying 'I will sing your praise in the midst of the assembly'. First Corinthians 14:15 and 14:26 set 'I will sing' (psalo) and 'a psalm' (psalmos) inside the gathered-church discourse where each member contributes a psalm for the building up of the body. James 5:13 makes singing the normal believer response paired with prayer. In the Old Testament Psalm 95:1 to 2 stacks first person plural 'let us' verbs (cohortatives): 'let us sing for joy' (neranenah), 'let us shout' (nariah), 'let us come before' (neqademah) him with 'thanksgiving' (todah) and 'with songs' (bizmirot); and Psalm 96:1 issues the plural command 'sing to the LORD a new song' (shiru), 'sing to the LORD all the earth'. Across both testaments the verbs are plural or reciprocal and the addressees are the assembly. So the lexicon firmly supports congregational singing as a commanded mode of worship. One word in the proposition, 'primary', claims that this mode ranks above other musical modes such as instrumental or choral music. The lexical data does not itself rank the modes, and a text like 1 Chronicles 25:7 shows trained instrumental musicians within Old Testament worship. So the evidence strongly affirms corporate singing as a worship mode the texts command, while the comparative claim that it is the primary mode rests on a weighing the lexicon alone cannot settle.
